analysis.one_liner: Taxes billionaires yearly on gains they haven't sold, ending tax-free deferral strategies like "buy, borrow, die."
analysis.headline: The Billionaires Income Tax Act, introduced in September 2025 with 23 cosponsors, was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill requires very wealthy households — those with over $100 million in annual income or over $1 billion in assets — to pay tax every year on the gains from their investments, even ones they haven't sold, the same way workers pay tax on every paycheck. It closes more than 30 tax rules that let the ultra-rich postpone or avoid taxes, including holding onto appreciating assets and borrowing against them tax-free, and passing assets to heirs without the gain ever being taxed. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways: directly, because the bill stops ultra-wealthy households from using strategies unavailable to wage earners, restoring a measure of equal treatment in the tax code; and indirectly, because the bill raises federal revenue from a few hundred very wealthy households rather than from broad-based taxes. Retirement accounts, 401(k)s, IRAs, 529 college savings plans, HSAs, and gifts to charity are all expressly exempt, so middle-class savers are not touched.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wage earners and the broader taxpaying public

how_it_helps.text: Applies mark-to-market taxation to "applicable taxpayers" — individuals with income over $100 million ($50 million if married filing separately) or assets over $1 billion for three straight years — treating unsold tradable investments as sold at market value each year so gains are taxed annually like wages. [S2]

Ends "buy, borrow, die": for hard-to-value assets like stakes in private companies, tax is triggered when the asset is transferred, with interest added for each year tax was deferred, capped at 49% of the gain. [S2]
Treats gifts, bequests, and trust transfers of covered assets as sales at fair market value, ending the step-up in basis that lets heirs sell inherited appreciated assets completely tax-free. [S2]

Modifies more than 30 additional tax provisions — like-kind exchanges, stock transfers, deferred compensation, private placement life insurance, opportunity funds, small business stock exclusions, and the net investment income tax — that currently shield high-net-worth income. [S2]
Keeps a 10-year tax grab on covered expatriates who renounce citizenship, making it harder to escape the tax by leaving. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The ultra-wealthy: roughly the few hundred households meeting the income or asset thresholds, plus their family trusts and the private companies they own stakes in. Wealth management, estate-planning, and tax-structuring businesses that earn fees building deferral strategies for these clients also lose business.

drawbacks.text: Mark-to-market taxation is hard to administer for illiquid assets: valuing private companies, farmland, and art every year requires estimates and heavy reporting, and the bill leans heavily on Treasury regulations to make it work. [S2]

Founders and owners of private companies could face tax bills on paper gains they cannot easily cash out; the bill softens this by allowing first-year taxes on nontradable assets to be paid in five annual installments and by letting owners defer tax on up to $1 billion of stock in a single company in exchange for an interest charge later, but the liquidity burden is real. [S2]

Critics question whether the Constitution's income-tax amendment permits taxing gains on assets that have not been sold at all — a live legal dispute over unrealized gains that could land in court. (General knowledge; the bill text itself addresses deferral but cannot settle the constitutional question.)

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a large amount of revenue and tax-system fairness, collected exclusively from households with nine or ten-figure fortunes, in exchange for significant administrative complexity and some legal uncertainty. The bill's carve-outs for retirement savings, charities, spouses, and installment payment on illiquid assets address the most serious fairness and liquidity objections, though the constitutional question over taxing unsold gains remains unresolved. On balance the benefits run to the broad public and the costs to a tiny slice of the wealthiest households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or any scheduled vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced S. 2845, the Billionaires Income Tax Act, on September 17, 2025. [S1] [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which is the only action it has received. [S4]
Twenty-three senators — 22 Democrats and one Independent — signed on as cosponsors; no Republican has. [S3]
With Republicans holding the Senate majority in the 119th Congress, the Finance Committee has taken no further action on the bill since referral. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The ultra-wealthy households the bill targets, and the wealth-management industry that serves them, are better off under the status quo: they keep the current deferral strategies, and no tax has been collected under the bill's terms.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors are Democrats or an Independent; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-run Senate Finance Committee has not moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill requires households with over $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets to pay tax annually on unrealized gains and closes the "buy, borrow, die" strategy and heir-basis step-up they currently use. Their interest in the status quo — paying little or no tax on paper wealth — comes at the direct expense of the federal revenue everyone else's taxes fund.

industries.industry: Private equity, venture capital, and founders of private companies
industries.note: Stakes in private companies are hard to value, so the bill taxes them at transfer with a deferral-recapture interest charge rather than annually, and limits deferral elections for significant owners. These investors' gain under current law is deferral of tax the public otherwise bears.

industries.industry: Wealth management, estate planning, and tax advisory
industries.note: These firms earn fees designing the deferral structures — private placement life insurance, grantor trusts, like-kind exchanges, opportunity funds — that the bill shuts down or restricts for applicable taxpayers. What is a service market for them is lost revenue for the Treasury.

industries.industry: Wall Street brokerages and securities dealers
industries.note: The bill creates new annual-valuation, reporting, and broker-statement obligations for tradable assets of applicable taxpayers, a compliance cost. Their clients are only the ultra-wealthy, and the valuation data they provide supports taxing gains the public now waits decades to collect.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support and the Finance Committee taking no action since referral in September 2025, the realistic path is that the bill stays in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress, as previous versions of this proposal have. Its main near-term use is as a stated position for a potential future Democratic majority.
